summary:
This is a website that connects Earth science with space exploration. A planetary analog site is an area on Earth that's geologically environmentally and or chemically similar to the surface of an important planet or moon in our solar system. We made sure to keep the explanation simple. We showcase two examples:

From Earth to Mars: The Atacama Desert in Chile is similar to Planum Boreum (the North Pole) on the surface of Mars. Its environment is extremely dry has radiation levels, big temperature swings (it gets very cold!). A high amount of perchlorate salts in the soil. All of this makes it the perfect place to test devices that will search for signs of life on Mars well as drilling equipment.

From Earth to the Moon: Devon Island, located in the Canadian Arctic is similar to Tycho Crater on the surface of the Moon. Both have a rocky surface and clear meteorite craters, with central peaks and melted rock. This makes it the best place to study geology and train rovers on how to navigate.
details: We built Planetary Mirrors as a web platform and early‑warning system that takes real‑time solar wind and coronal mass ejection data from NASA’s DONKI API and the DSCOVR satellite and turns it into clear geomagnetic storm forecasts. Planetary Mirrors uses a Python backend built with FastAPI and Scikit‑learn. Shows the magnetosphere in 3D with Three.js and React. Planetary Mirrors changes heliophysics information into a simple 1 to 5 risk scale and sends automatic alerts. Planetary Mirrors offers two modes: one for infrastructure operators and another for people. Planetary Mirrors also gives descriptions of solar wind and a very small low‑bandwidth version that is less, than 15 kilobytes. Because Planetary Mirrors is open source Planetary Mirrors lets power grid managers and satellite engineers get a 30‑to‑60‑minute warning that can save millions of dollars and stop blackouts. Planetary Mirrors makes space science simple and fun for everyone.
